Fix $K\ge2$. The input is a trained classifier with a measurable, finite-valued
logit map $z:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$, a nonempty finite validation sample
$(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^{n_v}$ with $n_v\ge1$ and $y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$, and a
finite nonempty set of candidate temperatures $\mathcal T\subset(0,\infty)$.
The validation labels were not used to fit the logits. For $T\in\mathcal T$,
compute
$$p_T(j\mid x)=\frac{\exp(z_j(x)/T)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K\exp(z_\ell(x)/T)}\quad (j=1,\ldots,K),\qquad L_{\mathrm{val}}(T)=-\frac1{n_v}\sum_{i=1}^{n_v}\log p_T(y_i\mid x_i).$$
Choose the smallest temperature among the minimizers,
$$T^*=\min\arg\min_{T\in\mathcal T}L_{\mathrm{val}}(T).$$
and return the forecasts $p_{T^*}(\cdot\mid x)$ and predicted label
$\min\arg\max_j p_{T^*}(j\mid x)$ for each input $x$. This is a
finite-candidate version of validation negative-log-likelihood temperature
scaling. It selects only by empirical validation loss; it makes no finite-sample
calibration guarantee for future data, particularly when the validation and
future data laws differ.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

derivations.claim: For every $j$, $w_j=\exp(z_j/T)$ is a finite positive real by [F2]. Hence $S=\sum_{\ell=1}^K w_\ell>0$, each $p_j(T)=w_j/S$ is positive, and $\sum_jp_j(T)=1$. Thus $p(T)$ is in the interior of $\Delta_K$.

For each validation example and class $j$, step 1.1 gives $p_T(j\mid x_i)>0$, so its logarithm is finite by [F4]. Thus each candidate loss is finite. The finite nonempty set $\mathcal T$ has a nonempty finite set of minimizers, which has a unique smallest element; the algorithm therefore returns a unique $T^*$.

For any classes $j,\ell$, positivity of $T$ preserves the sign of $z_j-z_\ell$. By [F3], $\exp(z_j/T)$ and $\exp(z_\ell/T)$ have the same strict order as $z_j$ and $z_\ell$; division by their common positive denominator $S$ from step 1.1 preserves that order and preserves ties. Every pairwise comparison is therefore identical for $p(T)$ and $z$, proving equality of their maximizing index sets.

citations.quote:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $K\ge2$, let
$Y:\Omega\to\{1,\ldots,K\}$ have the full power-set sigma-algebra, and let
$G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K):\Omega\to\Delta_K$ be a measurable random forecast, where
the probability simplex is
$\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_{j=1}^Kp_j=1\}$. Define the predicted label and
top confidence by
$$\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=\max_{\ell\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}G_\ell\},\qquad C=\max_{\ell\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}G_\ell.$$
The smallest-index rule resolves ties. The forecast is **top-label calibrated**
if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
Thus, among predictions whose top confidence lies in any specified set of
confidence values, the frequency of a correct top label equals the average
reported top confidence.

Let $K\ge2$ and let $(\widehat p_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be a nonempty finite
evaluation sample, where $\widehat p_i\in\Delta_K$ and
$y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$. For each $i$, let
$\widehat y_i=\min\arg\max_j\widehat p_{ij}$,
$c_i=\max_j\widehat p_{ij}$, and
$a_i=\mathbf 1_{\{\widehat y_i=y_i\}}$. Fix before evaluating the sample a
finite Borel partition $(B_1,\ldots,B_M)$ of $[0,1]$. For
$I_b=\{i:c_i\in B_b\}$ and $n_b=|I_b|>0$, define
$$\operatorname{acc}(B_b)=\frac1{n_b}\sum_{i\in I_b}a_i,\qquad \operatorname{conf}(B_b)=\frac1{n_b}\sum_{i\in I_b}c_i.$$
The **binned expected calibration error** and **binned maximum calibration
error** for this sample and partition are
$$\operatorname{ECE}_{(B_b)}=\sum_{b:n_b>0}\frac{n_b}{n}\left|\operatorname{acc}(B_b)-\operatorname{conf}(B_b)\right|,\qquad \operatorname{MCE}_{(B_b)}=\max_{b:n_b>0}\left|\operatorname{acc}(B_b)-\operatorname{conf}(B_b)\right|.$$
These are finite-sample, bin-dependent summaries, not the population expected
calibration error. They compare observed top-label accuracy with average
confidence within bins; log loss and Brier loss instead score probability
forecasts directly and are strictly proper.

Fix $K\ge2$. The input is a trained classifier with a measurable, finite-valued
logit map $z:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$, a nonempty finite validation sample
$(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^{n_v}$ with $n_v\ge1$ and $y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$, and a
finite nonempty set of candidate temperatures $\mathcal T\subset(0,\infty)$.
The validation labels were not used to fit the logits. For $T\in\mathcal T$,
compute
$$p_T(j\mid x)=\frac{\exp(z_j(x)/T)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K\exp(z_\ell(x)/T)}\quad (j=1,\ldots,K),\qquad L_{\mathrm{val}}(T)=-\frac1{n_v}\sum_{i=1}^{n_v}\log p_T(y_i\mid x_i).$$
Choose the smallest temperature among the minimizers,
$$T^*=\min\arg\min_{T\in\mathcal T}L_{\mathrm{val}}(T).$$
and return the forecasts $p_{T^*}(\cdot\mid x)$ and predicted label
$\min\arg\max_j p_{T^*}(j\mid x)$ for each input $x$. This is a
finite-candidate version of validation negative-log-likelihood temperature
scaling. It selects only by empirical validation loss; it makes no finite-sample
calibration guarantee for future data, particularly when the validation and
future data laws differ.

Let $K\ge2$, let $z\in\mathbb R^K$, and let $T>0$. Define
$$p_j(T)=\frac{\exp(z_j/T)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K\exp(z_\ell/T)}\quad (j=1,\ldots,K).$$
Then $p(T)$ lies in the interior of $\Delta_K$ and
$\arg\max_{j\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}p_j(T)
=\arg\max_{j\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}z_j$.
For the finite validation inputs and candidate temperatures specified in the
validation temperature-scaling algorithm, every validation loss is finite and
the stated smallest-minimizer rule returns a unique candidate.

Let $K\ge2$, let the feature space be a measurable space $\mathcal X$, and
let the label set be $\mathcal Y=\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with all subsets measurable.
Let $H$ be a training statistic valued in a measurable rule space $\mathcal H$,
and let $s:\mathcal H\times\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R$ be a
jointly measurable score rule. The rule is fixed after training and is used
unchanged on calibration and test examples. Given $m\ge0$ calibration examples
$(X_i,Y_i)$ and $0<\alpha<1$, compute
$$R_i=s(H,X_i,Y_i),\qquad k=\left\lceil(m+1)(1-\alpha)\right\rceil.$$
If $k\le m$, sort the calibration scores by the ordered keys $(R_i,i)$ and let
$q$ be the score value at position $k$. If $k=m+1$, set $q=+\infty$. For a
feature value $x$, return the prediction set
$$
C(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:s(H,x,y)\le q\}.
$$
For the optional tie-randomized version, use one random variable $U$ that is
uniform on $[0,1]$ and independent of the training information and all
calibration and test examples, shared across the candidate-label scan. For
$r_y=s(H,x,y)$, define
$$p_U(y)=\frac{\#\{i\le m:R_i>r_y\}+U\bigl(1+\#\{i\le m:R_i=r_y\}\bigr)}{m+1},\qquad C_U(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:p_U(y)>\alpha\}.$$
The candidate is included in its own tie group. The algorithm defines these
sets; any coverage claim requires separate distributional hypotheses.

Let $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$, $1\le i\le m+1$, be random elements of one measurable
example space $(\mathcal Z,\mathscr Z)$, and let $\mathcal T$ be the training
sigma-field. Suppose the tuple $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_{m+1})$ has a regular
conditional distribution $Q_\omega$ given $\mathcal T$ in the sense of
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], whose sections have joint laws
invariant under every coordinate permutation, as in
[[def-exchangeable-random-elements]], for almost every $\omega$. Let $H$ be a $\mathcal T$-measurable
training statistic, and let $s:\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$ be a
jointly measurable split score rule. Use the split set in
[[alg-split-conformal-prediction-set]] at $0<\alpha<1$. Then
$$\mathbb P\{Y_{m+1}\in C(X_{m+1})\mid\mathcal T\}\ge1-\alpha\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
If the tie-randomized set $C_U$ is used with one $U$ of Lebesgue probability
law on $[0,1]$ independent of $\mathcal T\vee\sigma(Z)$, then
$$\mathbb P\{Y_{m+1}\in C_U(X_{m+1})\mid\mathcal T\}=1-\alpha\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
In either case, integration over the training sigma-field gives the same
marginal lower bound or exact marginal coverage.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be random elements, $n\ge1$, of one measurable space
$(\mathcal Z,\mathscr Z)$. Their tuple $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ is a random element
of $(\mathcal Z^n,\mathscr Z^{\otimes n})$ by
[[lem-coordinate-maps-and-permutations-are-measurable-on-finite-products]],
and its law is the pushforward probability measure from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. For a permutation $\pi$ of
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$, let $\tau_\pi(z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$. The tuple is
**exchangeable** if
$$\mathbb P_Z\circ\tau_\pi^{-1}=\mathbb P_Z\qquad\text{for every permutation }\pi.$$

This is invariance of the joint law, not an assertion of independence or identical marginal construction by independent sampling. The coordinate maps $\tau_\pi$ are measurable by the cited finite-product lemma.

For every $K\ge2$ and $p,q\in\Delta_K$, the logarithmic and Brier losses in the definition of finite-label score loss satisfy $\bar S(p,p)\le\bar S(p,q)$, with equality only when $q=p$. The expected logarithmic loss at the truthful forecast is finite, including when some coordinates of $p$ vanish.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be nonempty measurable spaces. A **source/target pair of joint laws** consists of probability measures $P_S$ and $P_T$ on $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. For $D\in\{S,T\}$, its input marginal is the probability measure $\mu_D$ on $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ defined by $\mu_D(A)=P_D(A\times\mathsf Y)$. If $h:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ is measurable and $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ is product-measurable, then $(x,y)\mapsto(h(x),y)$ is measurable: the preimage of a measurable rectangle $U\times V$ is $h^{-1}(U)\times V$, and such rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. Taking preimages once more shows that $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(h(x),y)$ is measurable. The domain risk is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_D(h):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(h(x),y)\,P_D(d(x,y)).$$

A **conditional label kernel** for $P_D$ is a specified probability kernel $K_D$ from $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ such that, for every nonnegative product-measurable $g:\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int g(x,y)\,P_D(d(x,y))=\int_{\mathsf X}\left(\int_{\mathsf Y}g(x,y)\,K_D(x,dy)\right)\mu_D(dx).$$
The pair is under **covariate shift** when conditional label kernels $K_S,K_T$ are supplied, there is a measurable set $N$ with $\mu_T(N)=0$ such that $K_S(x,\cdot)=K_T(x,\cdot)$ as probability measures for every $x\notin N$, and $\mu_T\ll\mu_S$. No existence of conditional kernels is asserted by this definition.

derivations.claim: In the first model, $\widehat Y=1$ and $C=9/10$ almost surely. For $B=\{9/10\}$, the left side of [F1] is $1$ and the right side is $9/10$, so top-label calibration fails despite accuracy $1$. In the single occupied bin, [F2] gives both errors as $|1-9/10|=1/10$.

By [F10], temperature $1$ gives first-class probability $\exp(2\log3)/(1+\exp(2\log3))=9/10$, while temperature $2$ gives $\exp(\log3)/(1+\exp(\log3))=3/4$. The empirical NLL is the log-score risk $\bar S_{\log}(p,p_T)$ under the validation label frequencies $p=(3/4,1/4)$. Strict propriety [F9] therefore makes the value at $(3/4,1/4)$ strictly smaller than at $(9/10,1/10)$, so [F3] selects $T=2$. By [F4], both temperatures predict class $1$. Their one-bin gaps from the observed accuracy $3/4$ are $|3/4-9/10|=3/20$ and $|3/4-3/4|=0$.

In the rare-feature model, $m=1$ and $\alpha=1/2$ give $k=\lceil2(1/2)\rceil=1$, so the threshold is the single calibration score: it is $1$ for a rare calibration feature and $0$ for a common one. Write $Q$ for the finite joint law of the calibration and test pairs; by [A1], $Q(z_1,z_2)=\mu(z_1)\mu(z_2)$, which is unchanged by swapping coordinates. For the trivial training sigma-field, whose only events are $\emptyset$ and the whole space, the constant kernel with value $Q$ satisfies [F7]: the conditional-event integral is zero for $\emptyset$ and is the ordinary law identity for the whole space. By [F8] its section is exchangeable. The finite score rule is measurable, so [F6] applies and yields conditional-on-training marginal coverage at least $1/2$.

If the test feature is common, its true-label score is $0\le q$ for either possible threshold, so coverage is $1$. If it is rare, its true-label score is $1$, which is included exactly when the independent calibration feature is rare, an event of probability $1/10$. Thus subgroup coverage is $1/10$, while marginal coverage is $(9/10)\cdot1+(1/10)\cdot(1/10)=91/100$.

In the clean/corrupted model, the calibration score is always $0$, so $k=1$ gives $q=0$. At the target feature, both candidate labels have scores $1$ or $2$, hence neither belongs to $C(\mathrm{corrupted})$ and target coverage is $0$. The calibration/test pair law assigns mass one to (clean, corrupted) and zero to (corrupted, clean), so it is not invariant under swapping; the exchangeability hypothesis in [F6] fails.

finite_smoke.result: Top-label calibration fails on B={9/10}; one-bin ECE and MCE equal 1/10.

Marginal coverage is 91/100, but coverage given rare test feature is 1/10.
The source calibration threshold is 0 and target coverage is 0 because the true target label score is 1.
